title: Social Security Payments Will Rise 3.6 Percent in 2027
summary:
Millions of Americans who get Social Security payments will receive a raise next year. The Social Security Administration's yearly cost-of-living adjustment, often called the COLA, will be 3.6 percent for 2027, based on inflation data. The Associated Press reported that this amounts to a little more than $900 next year.

Social Security is a government program that sends monthly payments to people who are 62 or older and to people with a disability or blindness. Some family members of workers who have died can also receive payments.

The COLA is a math formula tied to consumer prices. It is meant to help payments keep up with inflation, which is the rise in the cost of everyday things. The Bureau of Labor Statistics compares average prices from July through September with the same months a year earlier. When inflation is high, the COLA is bigger. When inflation is low, it is smaller. The new amount takes effect in January.

Shai Akabas of the Bipartisan Policy Center said next year's increase is "not wildly outside of the norm." He explained that inflation has stayed above the Federal Reserve's 2 percent goal since 2021, so recent COLAs have also been higher.

Experts said the raise may not feel the same for everyone. Older adults often spend more on health care than younger people, and the formula is based on the costs of working city residents, not retired people. Akabas said a rise in Medicare costs could take a bite out of the increase. He also said that because gas prices are high, people who drive a lot may feel the raise is not enough.

In a poll by the group AARP, about 7 in 10 older adults said an increase between 5 and 8 percent would be enough to help with expenses.
why_it_matters: Millions of older Americans depend on Social Security, so the size of the yearly raise affects whether they can keep up with rising prices.

Medicare is a U.S. government health insurance program mainly for people 65 and older.

background_read: Social Security is a U.S. government program that pays monthly benefits, mostly to retired workers, using money collected from workers' paychecks.
Because prices tend to rise over time, a fixed payment would buy less each year, so Social Security adds a yearly cost-of-living adjustment.
The adjustment is figured with a formula based on consumer prices from July through September, compared with the same months a year earlier.
Many older people rely on these payments for rent, food and health care, so the size of the yearly raise matters to millions of households.
